title: The Swahili coast
hookLine: Kilwa, Lamu and Zanzibar, stone towns of Muslim traders on the Indian Ocean

lines: ASKED FOR THE CLOTHES OFF HIS BACK.
cards: A poor man walks up to the sultan of Kilwa after Friday prayer and asks him for the clothes he is wearing. Not money. The clothes.

The sultan doesn't laugh him off. He goes home, changes, and gives the man the very clothes off his back. Ibn Battuta was in the town and tells the story, and says the sultan was known for his giving.
Kilwa is on the other side of Africa from everything this week: not the desert, but the Indian Ocean coast, among towns where the sea, not the sand, carried everything in. Today: the Swahili coast.

teach.h: STONE TOWNS ON ISLANDS AND INLETS.
teach.b: Along Africa's east coast, from what is now Somalia down toward Mozambique, Muslim trading towns grew up on islands and inlets: Kilwa, Mombasa, Lamu, Zanzibar, and more.
They were built of coral stone cut from the reef, with carved wooden doors and mosques by the water. Ibn Battuta called Kilwa one of the most beautiful and well-built towns he had seen.
What made these towns possible was the wind.

teach.h: THE MONSOON TURNS, THE SHIPS WAIT.
teach.b: The monsoon blows one way for part of the year and the other way for the rest. Ships from Arabia, Persia and India rode it down to Africa, waited for the wind to turn, and rode it home. In the waiting, traders stayed.
They married into local families, prayed in local mosques, and a coastal Muslim culture grew, with its own language, Swahili, an African language rich in words borrowed from Arabic.
The Qur'an counts the winds and the ships among God's signs: it speaks of winds sent as bearers of good news, so that the ships may sail by God's command and people may seek His bounty.
On this coast, that was simply the shape of the year.

So ends one week: the Sahara's salt, gold and books; the empire of Mali; Mansa Musa's Hajj; Timbuktu's manuscripts; Djenné's mud mosque; Songhay's askia; and now the coast, where faith arrived by sea.

how: Muslims on the Swahili coast pray in old coral-stone mosques in towns like Lamu and Zanzibar, and Swahili is spoken across East Africa.

games.q: you're a trader from Arabia in a coastal town of East Africa. the wind has turned and won't carry you home for a long while. what do you do?
o: sit on your ship and wait.
stay, trade, pray in the town's mosque, and get to know its families.
try to sail against the wind.
games.why: traders waiting for the monsoon stayed, married into local families and prayed in local mosques. the coast's Muslim culture grew out of that waiting.

practice: Picture a map: the east coast of Africa, then the Arabian Peninsula, then India, and trace a line across the water between them and back again, one trader's year, out with one wind and home with the other.
Breathe in as you trace out, and out as you trace back. If you pray, remember those who traveled that water and prayed on its shores; if not, simply feel the rhythm of going and returning.

wordCard.voice: Swahili. The language and culture that grew along Africa's Indian Ocean coast, from Kilwa to Lamu and Zanzibar, whose year turned with the monsoon wind. Today's word.
